artworks.title: Thyestes and Aerope
artworks.description: Nosadella paints Thyestes with Aerope — the brother who stole Atreus' wife and the golden fleece token of the Mycenaean throne. The Bolognese canvas stages the adultery that precedes the feast: desire and usurpation before the children are served. Oil on canvas.

artworks.title: Atreus and Thyestes (Urbino maiolica)
artworks.description: Urbino istoriato ware sets Thyestes opposite his brother across the curse that will end at table. The maiolica plate turns the Pelopid feud into a bright ceramic narrative — Thyestes as the guest who does not yet know what he will eat. Tin-glazed earthenware.

artworks.title: The Feast of Atreus and Thyestes
artworks.artist: Václav Jindřich Nosecký and Michael Wenzel Halbax
artworks.description: The Zákupy Castle mural stages Seneca's horror: Thyestes at the banquet where Atreus serves him his own sons. The painting freezes the moment the house of Pelops becomes proverb — the guest who eats what no guest should. Wall painting, Zákupy Castle.

artworks.title: The Killing of Atreus
artworks.description: An Apulian vase shows the sequel to the feast: Atreus slain in the feud Thyestes' bloodline continues. The killing closes the circle the banquet opened — Thyestes' revenge cycle outliving the meal that made his name. South Italian pottery.

popCulture.title: Thyestes
popCulture.creator: Seneca the Younger
popCulture.description: Seneca's blood-dark tragedy stages the feast itself — Atreus' vengeance served at table — and became the model horror-play of the European stage, from Elizabethan revenge drama onward.

popCulture.title: Thyestean feast
popCulture.description: The banquet survived as a phrase: a "Thyestean feast" names any meal of unspeakable flesh — the house of Pelops condensed into an adjective.
